PHSCS 587

Strain engineering

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how an illustrative strain-induced valley splitting changes carrier occupancy

Strain changes the crystal lattice and therefore its electronic bands. It may lift valley degeneracy, change band curvature and alter inter-valley scattering. Carrier populations can move toward bands that conduct more effectively along a chosen direction.

Near a parabolic band edge, the inverse conductivity effective mass is related to band curvature by 1/m* = (1/ℏ²)d²E/dk² along the transport direction. Effective mass is directional; it is not the electron’s free-space rest mass.

Tensile and compressive, uniaxial and biaxial stress have different effects on electrons and holes. A useful engineering statement identifies the material, crystal orientation, stress direction and carrier type. It does not assume any strain improves every device.

Example

In a simplified μ = qτ/m* model, reducing transport effective mass by 20% at unchanged scattering time τ raises mobility by 1/0.8 = 1.25. Real strain can change τ and occupancy too, so this is a single-mechanism estimate.

Sources and scope
  • PHSCS 587 reading: 5.2, strain effect on mobility
  • PHSCS 587, 5.2 recording 1: lattice strain, valley occupation and transport mass.

Practice

1. Why is “strain reduces effective mass” an incomplete performance argument?

Consider occupancy, transport direction and scattering as well as curvature.

The occupied bands, directional mass and scattering time jointly determine transport. A favorable curvature change can be offset or enhanced by the other changes.
